title: Relative pronouns: qui, que, où, dont
topic: relative pronouns; ce qui / ce que
why: Relative pronouns are what turn short sentences into precise, natural ones: the colleague who, the book that, the day when. This lesson explains qui, que, où and dont by contrast with English, where that is often dropped and prepositions end up at the end of the sentence.

Qui and que

Relative pronouns let you build longer, more precise sentences: “the colleague who works with me”, “the book that I'm reading”. English chooses between who, which and that depending on whether it's a person or a thing. French doesn't care about that: it chooses depending on the role of the pronoun in its clause.

pronounrolewhat followsexample
quisubjecta verble collègue qui travaille avec moi
que / qu'direct objecta subject + verble collègue que je vois tous les jours

The quick test: look at the word right after the gap. If it's a verb, it's qui: la femme qui parle. If it's a subject (je, tu, Paul, les enfants…), it's que: la femme que Paul connaît. And it works the same for people and things: le train qui part, le train que je prends.

J'ai une amie qui habite à Rennes.I have a friend who lives in Rennes.
C'est le livre que je lis en ce moment.It's the book (that) I'm reading at the moment.
Le film qu'on a vu hier était génial.The movie we saw yesterday was great.

The big trap for English speakers: English can drop “that”: “the book I'm reading”, “the man I met”. French never drops que: le livre que je lis, l'homme que j'ai rencontré. Without it, the sentence is simply wrong.

Que becomes qu' before a vowel (qu'il, qu'on, qu'elle). Qui never elides: l'ami qui arrive, never “qu'arrive”.

", "

Où and dont

Où: where… and when

Où introduces a place, as in English: la ville où j'habite (the town where I live). But it also introduces a moment, where English uses “when” or nothing at all:

Lyon, c'est la ville où je suis né.Lyon is the city where I was born.
Le jour où je suis arrivé à Paris, il pleuvait.The day (when) I arrived in Paris, it was raining.
C'était l'année où on a acheté la maison.It was the year we bought the house.

Never use quand after a noun of time: “le jour quand” is a typical English speaker's mistake. Say le jour où, le moment où, l'été où.

Dont: replacing de + noun

Dont replaces a complement introduced by de. Think of the verbs and expressions with de you know: parler de, avoir besoin de, s'occuper de, avoir envie de, être content de.

with dewith dont
Je parle de ce film.le film dont je parle (the film I'm talking about)
J'ai besoin de cet outil.l'outil dont j'ai besoin (the tool I need)
Je m'occupe de ce projet.le projet dont je m'occupe (the project I'm in charge of)

Dont also translates “whose”: la femme dont le fils est médecin (the woman whose son is a doctor). Careful, no possessive after it: not “dont son fils”.

English often ends the sentence with a preposition: “the film I'm talking about”, “the tool I need”. French can't do that: the de moves to the front and becomes dont.

", "

Ce qui, ce que, and agreement

When English says “what” in the middle of a sentence (not a question), French uses ce qui or ce que, with the same rule as qui and que: a verb follows → ce qui; a subject follows → ce que.

Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est l'histoire.What interests me is history.
Ce que je veux, c'est un café.What I want is a coffee.
Je ne comprends pas ce que tu dis.I don't understand what you're saying.
Dis-moi ce qui ne va pas.Tell me what's wrong.

The structure Ce que…, c'est… is very common in speech to highlight something: Ce que j'aime à Bordeaux, c'est la Garonne. Never use quoi here: “je ne sais pas quoi tu veux” is wrong; say je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.

Agreement after que

You know the rule from unit 10: with avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object placed before it. Que is exactly that: a direct object placed before the verb. So the participle agrees with the noun que stands for.

nounexample
la robe (fem. sing.)la robe que j'ai achetée
les photos (fem. pl.)les photos que tu as prises
les gâteaux (masc. pl.)les gâteaux qu'elle a faits

Most of the time you can't hear the agreement (achetée sounds like acheté), but with participles ending in a consonant you can: prise, mise, faite, écrite. La lettre qu'il a écrite: the t is pronounced.
